questions.prompt: What does the "GPT" in GPT stand for?
options: General Processing Tool
Generative Pre-trained Transformer
Guided Prompt Technology
Global Pattern Tracker
questions.explanation: Generative (it produces output), Pre-trained (trained on large text corpora before you ever use it), Transformer (the neural network architecture underneath).

questions.prompt: The transformer architecture behind modern language models was introduced in a 2017 paper called:
options: Deep Residual Learning
Attention Is All You Need
Generative Adversarial Networks
Language Models Are Few-Shot Learners
questions.explanation: "Attention Is All You Need" (Vaswani et al., 2017) introduced the transformer. Nearly every large language model in use today descends from it.

questions.prompt: In language-model terms, a "token" is closest to:
options: One complete sentence
One letter
A chunk of text, often part of a word
One paragraph
questions.explanation: Models read and write in tokens, which are word fragments. A long word may be several tokens; a common short word is usually one.

options: How much text it can consider at one time
How long it has been in production
The screen area the chat occupies
The number of users it can serve at once
questions.explanation: Everything the model is working with — your instructions, attached documents, the conversation so far — competes for the same window. Once it is full, the earliest material falls out of view.

questions.prompt: Raising the "temperature" setting on a model does what?
options: Makes it answer faster
Makes its output more varied and less predictable
Increases the factual accuracy
Expands the context window
questions.explanation: Temperature controls how much randomness is allowed when picking the next token. Low values give repeatable, conservative output; high values give variety, and more risk of drift.

options: Runs in several data centres
Can be fine-tuned more than once
Works with more than one kind of input, such as text and images
Supports several languages
questions.explanation: Modalities are kinds of data: text, images, audio, video. A multimodal model handles more than one, so it can read a floor plan or a scanned lease rather than only typed text.

options: The point where training was stopped to save cost
The date after which it has no built-in knowledge of events
The maximum size of a document it will accept
The limit on how many questions you may ask
questions.explanation: Anything after the cutoff is unknown to the model unless you give it the information or connect it to a live source. This is why a confident answer about recent events deserves checking.

questions.prompt: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mainly solves which problem?
options: The model is too slow
The model does not know your private or current documents
The model uses too much electricity
The model cannot write code
questions.explanation: RAG fetches relevant passages from your own content and puts them in the context window before the model answers. The model is not retrained; it is simply handed the right material.

questions.prompt: Fine-tuning differs from prompting because fine-tuning:
options: Changes the model itself by training it further on examples
Gives the model more time to think
Is a different word for writing a longer prompt
Only works on open-source models
questions.explanation: Prompting shapes one conversation; fine-tuning adjusts the model's weights using example pairs, so the behaviour persists. It is far more expensive, and for most business problems prompting or RAG gets there first.

questions.prompt: Which best describes an AI "agent" rather than a chatbot?
options: It responds faster
It takes actions toward a goal, not just produces text
It runs on the user's own device
It has a larger context window
questions.explanation: An agent can call tools, read and write systems, and chain several steps together. The practical consequence is that the review step moves from every output to a sample.

questions.prompt: Prompt injection is an attack where:
options: Someone guesses your password from a prompt
Instructions hidden in content the model reads cause it to misbehave
Too many prompts are sent at once to overload the service
The model is trained on poisoned data
questions.explanation: If a model reads a web page, email or document, text inside that content can pose as instructions. It matters far more once the model can act, because a bad instruction then has consequences beyond a wrong answer.

questions.prompt: "Hallucination" in this context means the model:
options: Crashes unexpectedly
Refuses to answer
States something false with complete confidence
Repeats the same answer twice
questions.explanation: The output is fluent, well-formatted and wrong. Fluency is exactly what makes it hard to catch, which is why fact-bearing output needs a reviewer who knows the subject.

questions.prompt: The main risk of pasting internal documents into a personal, unapproved AI account is:
options: The answer will be lower quality
Company data leaves your control and your retention rules
It uses more of your mobile data
The file may be reformatted
questions.explanation: Once the content sits in an account the organisation does not administer, nobody can say where it is stored, how long it is kept, or who else can reach it.

options: Models that run without internet access
Employees using AI tools the organisation has not approved
A backup model that takes over on failure
AI used to detect other AI
questions.explanation: It is worth measuring rather than punishing. A large gap between the sanctioned tools and the used ones usually means the sanctioned ones are not good enough or not available.

questions.prompt: An AI incident log with zero entries after a year of real use most likely means:
options: The deployment is working flawlessly
Nobody is recording incidents
The use cases are too simple to fail
Staff are satisfied with the tools
questions.explanation: A clean log is nearly always a reporting gap rather than a safety record. The first useful governance metric is whether anyone has anywhere to report a problem.

questions.prompt: If an AI tool drafts a clause that turns out to be wrong, accountability sits with:
options: The model vendor
The person and organisation that used and relied on the output
Nobody, since the output was automated
The employee who wrote the prompt, personally
questions.explanation: Across essentially every governance framework, using an output is adopting it. Vendor terms disclaim it, and "the system produced it" has never been a defence.

questions.prompt: Before deploying AI to a process, the most commonly skipped step is:
options: Choosing the right model
Measuring how the process performs today
Writing a prompt library
Negotiating the licence
questions.explanation: Without a baseline captured beforehand, every efficiency claim afterwards is an estimate. It is the cheapest step and the one that makes every later number defensible.

questions.prompt: The strongest reason to keep a human review step on AI output is that models:
options: Work slowly without supervision
Fail in ways that look plausible
Cannot format documents correctly
Need approval for legal reasons only
questions.explanation: A calculator fails loudly and obviously. A language model fails smoothly, in well-written prose, which means detecting the failure takes roughly the expertise the tool was meant to save.
